RagShortTexts: The 1054 Schism and Fourth Crusade plunder left deep theological rifts between East and West.

Variants.Content: The mutual excommunications of 1054 stayed in force for centuries, and the rift became a matter of money as much as theology. Venetian merchants held privileges in Constantinople under the chrysobull of 1082, and local craftsmen watched Latin ships take the harbor's profits. Doctrinal quarrels over the filioque clause and papal primacy hardened as each side labeled the other's rites heretical. The 1204 sack by Fourth Crusaders turned that resentment into lasting hatred, because Greek chroniclers remembered crusaders stripping the altars of churches. Any reunion treaty had to settle both a theological question and a fiscal one, and the union agreed at Lyon in 1274 was rejected by much of the Byzantine clergy.

Michael VIII explored diplomatic church union to stave off western crusades, but Byzantine clergy vehemently resisted papal submission, proclaiming they preferred the Turkish turban to the Latin mitre.
Commoners care little for abstract scholastic grammar, but know Latins use unleavened bread for communion. Crossing themselves with three fingers instead of two can incite tavern brawls.
